hints: Start by thinking about the central flow of information in cells - what does a gene normally do to produce a trait?
Huntington's is dominant, so ask yourself how many copies of the mutant allele are needed and what part of the gene is expanded.
Link the changed DNA sequence to the protein - what happens to the structure and function of huntingtin protein?
Finish by connecting the faulty protein to what you actually see in a person - which body system is damaged and what symptoms result?
walkthrough:
Start With The Gene**
Think of a gene as a recipe for a protein. In Huntington's disease the recipe itself is changed. There is a mutation in the HTT gene that codes for the protein huntingtin, involving extra CAG repeats. It is dominant, so having just one copy of the mutant allele in a heterozygote is enough to cause the disease.

From Gene To Faulty Protein**
Because the DNA base sequence is changed, transcription and translation produce an altered amino acid sequence. The result is a non-functional or toxic form of huntingtin protein that cannot carry out its normal role in nerve cells.

From Protein To Phenotype**
Phenotype means the observable effect. Faulty huntingtin damages neurones, especially in the brain. That is why the symptoms are changes in cognition, behaviour, personality and mood, plus loss of coordination and difficulties with movement.

Final answer: Mutation of the HTT / huntingtin gene with increased CAG repeats; dominant so only one mutant allele needed for disease. Non-functional / altered huntingtin protein produced. Leads to disease phenotype of cognitive / behavioural / personality changes and loss of coordination / movement difficulties.

hints: Look carefully at Fig. 2.1 and list who shows the disease - are they males, females, or both?
Recall which sex chromosomes males and females have - who is the only one to carry a Y chromosome?
Trace the path from fathers to children - which children always inherit their father's Y chromosome and what is their phenotype?
walkthrough:
Spot The Pattern In The Pedigree**
The first clue is very simple. In Fig. 2.1 every affected person is male. No females develop retinitis pigmentosa in this family. That already suggests the allele is not on an autosome or on the X chromosome, where you would expect some females to be affected.

Link Sex To Chromosomes**
Remember that biological males are XY and females are XX. Only males possess a Y chromosome. If a gene is on the Y chromosome, only males can possibly inherit and show it.

Check Father To Son Inheritance**
A father passes his Y chromosome to all his sons and his X chromosome to all his daughters. In the pedigree, all sons of affected males are affected. That perfect father to son transmission matches Y-linkage exactly.

Final answer: Only males show the disease, females do not. Only males have a Y chromosome (XY), females are XX. All sons of affected fathers have the disease, showing father to son transmission of the Y chromosome.

hints: Write down the two parental genotypes first - what is the genotype of a healthy XY father and a heterozygous affected mother?
Work out the gametes each parent can make by separating the sex chromosomes and X alleles.
Set up a Punnett square to combine male and female gametes and read off the four offspring genotypes.
Remember dominance - any individual with $X^A$ shows the disease, so link each genotype to its phenotype to get the ratio.
walkthrough:
Define The Parents**
A healthy father must be $X^a Y$ because he has only one X chromosome and it must carry the normal recessive allele. A heterozygous affected mother must be $X^A X^a$ because the disease is dominant and she has one disease allele and one normal allele.

Build The Punnett Square**
The mother makes two types of egg: $X^A$ and $X^a$. The father makes two types of sperm: $X^a$ and Y. Put them on the sides of a 2 x 2 square and combine:
$$X^A X^a$, $X^a X^a$, $X^A Y$, $X^a Y$$

Convert Genotypes To Phenotypes**
Because $X^A$ is dominant, anyone with $X^A$ shows incontinentia pigmenti. So $X^A X^a$ is an affected female, $X^a X^a$ is a normal female, $X^A Y$ is an affected male, $X^a Y$ is a normal male. Each class is equally likely, giving a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 phenotypic ratio.

Final answer: Parents: $X^A X^a$ x $X^a Y$; gametes: $X^A$, $X^a$ and $X^a$, Y. Offspring: $X^A X^a$ affected female, $X^a X^a$ normal female, $X^A Y$ affected male, $X^a Y$ normal male. Expected phenotypic ratio 1 affected female : 1 normal female : 1 affected male : 1 normal male (1:1:1:1).

hints: Start with the normal job of a repressor - where does it bind and what does it stop?
Imagine the repressor is missing or cannot bind - what will now happen to transcription of the structural genes?
Now imagine the opposite fault where the repressor binds too tightly and never leaves - what essential product will be missing and how could either error damage the cell?
walkthrough:
Recall How A Repressor Works**
A regulatory gene codes for a repressor protein that binds to the operator site next to structural genes. When bound, it blocks RNA polymerase, so the structural genes are switched off and no mRNA or protein is made.

When The Repressor Fails**
If the mutation means no repressor is made, or a faulty repressor cannot bind the operator, the switch is stuck on. Structural genes are transcribed continuously and their proteins or enzymes are made in excess. If those proteins are harmful or disrupt metabolism, they damage the cell and cause disease.

When The Repressor Sticks Too Tightly**
The opposite fault is also possible. The mutant repressor may bind more tightly than normal and never release. Then structural genes stay switched off, their useful proteins or enzymes are never made, and the lack of that essential product disrupts metabolism and causes disease.

Final answer: Any three from: mutant regulatory gene makes no / faulty repressor that fails to bind operator, so structural genes are transcribed / switched on and harmful proteins / enzymes made that damage cell / alter metabolism; OR altered repressor binds too tightly to operator, so structural genes stay switched off and lack of essential protein / enzyme causes cell damage / disease.
